To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
cross-project defect prediction is hard and the success of cross- project defect prediction depends on the domain, the process, and the amount of training data.

(i) the success of crossproject prediction is highly unpredictable, (ii) there is little evidence for the success of domain-based or process-based transfer, and (iii) cross-project defect prediction is possible but only if the target project is very similar to the source project.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
cross-project prediction works well only in a few specific cases, and that there are no general guidelines that can be followed.
cross-project defect prediction is not a viable alternative to within-project defect prediction, but it is possible to identify projects for which cross-project prediction is feasible.

cross-project prediction can be successful, but only if the models are trained with data from the application that is to be predicted and the data is from a project that is similar to the one for which the prediction is to be made.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the success of crossproject prediction is highly dependent on the domain of the projects.
cross-project defect prediction is a challenge and that there is no silver bullet to solve the problem.
cross-project defect prediction is hard and should be used with great caution.
The main takeaway from our work is that
cross-project defect prediction is possible, but only if the right models are selected.
the choice of the source project is the single most influential factor for cross-project defect prediction, and that it is more important than the domain or process.
cross-project prediction can be successful, but it requires a good understanding of the data, process, and domain of the target application.
